In [[mathematics]], in the area of [[potential theory]], a '''Lebesgue spine''' or '''Lebesgue thorn''' is a type of [[Set (mathematics)|set]] used for discussing solutions to the [[Dirichlet problem]] and related problems of potential theory. The Lebesgue spine was introduced in 1912 by [[Henri Lebesgue]] to demonstrate that the Dirichlet problem does not always have a solution, particularly when the boundary has a sufficiently sharp edge protruding into the interior of the region.

== Definition ==

A typical Lebesgue spine in <math>\R^n</math>, for <math>n\ge 3,</math> is defined as follows
:<math>S = \{(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n)\in\R^n : x_n>0, x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots
+x_{n-1}^2 \le \exp(-1/x_n^2) \}.</math>

The important features of this set are that it is [[Connected set|connected]] and [[path-connected]] in the [[euclidean topology]] in <math>\R^n</math> and the origin is a [[limit point]] of the set, and yet the set is thin at the origin, as defined in the article [[Fine topology (potential theory)]].

== Observations ==

The set <math>S</math> is not closed in the [[euclidean topology]] since it does not contain the origin which is a [[limit point]] of <math>S</math>, but the set is closed in the [[Fine topology (potential theory)|fine topology]] in <math>\R^n</math>.

In comparison, it is not possible in <math>\R^2</math> to construct such a connected set which is thin at the origin.
